title: Needs and wants
job: Say what you want and don't want
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: Asking for something is two moves: name it, finish with juseyo. mul juseyo, keopi juseyo. The object marker -eul/-reul can go on the thing — mul-eul juseyo — and in a short spoken order it usually does not. There is no word for 'please' floating in the sentence — the politeness is inside juseyo itself.

Wanting to do something is built on the verb STEM: take meokda ('eat'), put -go on the stem to get meokgo, and follow it with sipeoyo. The object still comes first, with or without its marker, and the whole want lands at the end of the sentence.

isseoyo covers both 'there is' and 'I have', and eopseoyo covers both 'there is not' and 'I do not have'. English splits those into two constructions; Korean has one, and what exists takes -i or -ga rather than the object marker.

eopseoyo is a word in its own right, not isseoyo with something added. You cannot make it by putting an in front — an isseoyo is not how absence is said. Two verbs, one for presence and one for absence, and both have to be learned.

an means 'not' and it stands in FRONT of the verb: cha-reul an masyeoyo. It is the only piece in this course that goes before what it belongs to — every marker you have met so far attaches behind its word.

Korean has three ways of saying 'not' and this course teaches one. an is plain negation. mot says you are unable to for reasons outside you, and a longer form built on the verb's own ending says much the same as an with a different weight. You will hear both; they are for a later level.

-do ('too') REPLACES the marker on its noun instead of stacking with it: keopi-do juseyo, never keopi-reul-do juseyo. English keeps 'coffee' and adds 'also' somewhere else in the sentence, which is exactly the habit that produces the double marker.

When the thing you want to eat or drink carries a marker, it is the OBJECT marker, even though the verb of the sentence is 'want': bap-eul meokgo sipeoyo. The marker belongs to eating, not to wanting. In short everyday speech it is dropped — bap meokgo sipeoyo — and both are right.
Where the situation says who, the subject disappears. bap an meogeoyo is a complete sentence about yourself; jeo-neun is added only when you are marking yourself out from somebody else.

words.note: 'Water'. Asking for it is the first thing most travellers need, and mul juseyo is the whole request; mul-eul juseyo, with the object marker, is the same request said a shade more carefully.
'Please give me' — the whole of asking for something: name the thing, finish with juseyo. A marker on the thing is optional in a short order. The -se- inside is the respectful piece of jinaeseyo.

sentences.trap: There is no word in this sentence meaning 'please'. English hangs politeness off a separate word; Korean puts it inside the verb, so hunting for a word to add is hunting for something that is already there.
sentences.sound: mul JOO-se-yo. The l at the end of mul is held with the tongue tip up — not the dark English l. When a marker follows it, as in mul-eul, it softens into an r sound and the two run together as moo-rul; that linking happens every time a word ending in a consonant takes a marker beginning with a vowel.

variations.changed: the object marker on — correct, and a shade more careful than the bare noun
a different thing asked for
-do on the noun: you are adding water to something already ordered

mistake.why: The verb has been put first, English-style — 'give me water'. juseyo is the verb, so it is the last word; the thing you want stands in front of it.

sentences.usage: Ordering anything at all, in a cafe, a shop or a home.
sentences.mnemonic: Name it, ask for it — two words is a whole request.

words.note: 'Coffee', from M1, wearing two new markers here: -do for 'coffee too' and -ga for coffee as the thing that exists.
'Too'. It REPLACES the marker rather than joining it: keopi-reul juseyo becomes keopi-do juseyo, never keopi-reul-do. English adds 'also' and leaves the rest alone — a habit to break.
'Please give me' — the whole of asking for something: name the thing, finish with juseyo. A marker on the thing is optional in a short order. The -se- inside is the respectful piece of jinaeseyo.

sentences.trap: In English 'also' is a separate word that can go almost anywhere in the sentence. In Korean it is an ending, and it takes the place of the marker that would otherwise be there — so nothing is added and something is swapped.
sentences.sound: KUH-pee-do JOO-se-yo. -do is one short beat, said no louder than anything around it. It never carries emphasis by being said harder; it carries it by being there at all.

variations.changed: the same ending on a consonant-final noun — -do never changes shape
a third noun, and still one ending
the plain request, for comparison — 'too' simply comes off

mistake.why: Both endings have been put on, one after the other. -do does not stack; it stands where -reul would have stood, and only one of them can be there.

sentences.mnemonic: -do does not join the marker — it takes its seat.

words.note: 'Cooked rice', and by extension a meal: bap meokgo sipeoyo is closer to 'I want to eat' than 'I want rice'. Korean counts the day in meals of bap as English does in breakfast and dinner.
'Eat'. Two shapes of one verb: meogeoyo is the plain -yo form used from the next module on; meokgo is the shape before sipeoyo. The stem is meok-, and everything happens to that.
'Want to'. It never stands alone: it follows a verb wearing -go, and the two together are the wanting. The verb ends the clause anyway, so sipeoyo is the last thing in the sentence.

sentences.trap: English builds 'want to eat' with an infinitive: want, then to, then eat. Korean has no 'to' at all — the -go on the verb does that work, and the wanting comes last, after the thing being eaten. Nobody says 'I' here either: the sentence is about you unless something says otherwise.
sentences.sound: bap MUK-go SI-puh-yo. The p at the end of bap is held, not released — the lips close and the next word follows. meokgo has a hard k running into g; sipeoyo has the eo vowel again — 'puh', not 'po'.

variations.changed: the object marker on — correct, and what a careful sentence looks like
jeo-neun added — only when you are setting yourself against somebody who does not
the same words with a rise, asked of the person in front of you

mistake.why: The wanting has been moved to the front, English-style. sipeoyo is the verb of the sentence, so it goes last; nothing at all follows it.

sentences.usage: Saying what you would like to do, in a restaurant or at home.
sentences.mnemonic: The verb wears -go, the wanting waits at the end.

words.note: 'Water'. Asking for it is the first thing most travellers need, and mul juseyo is the whole request; mul-eul juseyo, with the object marker, is the same request said a shade more carefully.
'Drink'. Stem masi-; the plain -yo form and the -go shape before sipeoyo. The stem's i and the ending run together into masyeoyo — a normal contraction, written as it is said.
'Want to'. It never stands alone: it follows a verb wearing -go, and the two together are the wanting. The verb ends the clause anyway, so sipeoyo is the last thing in the sentence.

sentences.trap: The object keeps its -eul even though the main verb is 'want'. The marker belongs to the drinking, not to the wanting, and it stays exactly where the drinking put it.
sentences.sound: MOO-rul ma-SI-go SI-puh-yo. mul runs into -eul as moo-rul. masigo keeps the stem's i clearly; it is only in the plain form masyeoyo that the i and the ending run together. Both are the same verb.

variations.changed: a different drink, and -reul after the vowel
the marker dropped, which is how it is said over a counter
jeo-neun added — 'me, I want water', when others want something else

mistake.why: The finished -yo form has been put in front of sipeoyo. sipeoyo follows the -go shape of the verb — masigo — and nothing else; two -yo endings in one clause is two verbs.

sentences.usage: Saying what you would like to drink.
sentences.mnemonic: Mark the object for the verb that does the acting, not for the one that wants.

words.note: 'Korean', the language, from M1 — and here it is the thing being learned, so it takes -eul.
'Learn'. Stem baeu-, and again two shapes: baewoyo on its own, baeugo in front of sipeoyo. It takes an object with -eul or -reul, exactly as English 'learn' takes one.
'Want to'. It never stands alone: it follows a verb wearing -go, and the two together are the wanting. The verb ends the clause anyway, so sipeoyo is the last thing in the sentence.

sentences.trap: There is no shorter way to say this. English can say 'I want Korean' and be understood; Korean needs the verb, because hangungmal is a thing and wanting a thing is not the same construction as wanting to do something.
sentences.sound: han-GOONG-ma-rul BAE-oo-go SI-puh-yo. The l of -mal links into the -eul as it did in mul-eul, so the start of the sentence runs as ma-rul. baeugo has three clear beats, none of them stressed.

variations.changed: somebody else wanting it — the verb does not change for the person
jeo-neun added — when it is you as against somebody else

variations.cue: Do you want to learn Korean?
variations.changed: the marker dropped and a rise added — asked of the person in front of you

mistake.why: The verb has been thrown away and sipeoyo left to want a noun on its own. It cannot: sipeoyo only ever follows a verb wearing -go. Wanting a thing is said another way, and it is not this.

sentences.usage: Saying what you are trying to learn.
sentences.mnemonic: sipeoyo never wants a thing — it wants an action.

words.note: 'Friend', from M1, and here it is what exists: chingu-ga isseoyo, 'I have a friend'. The -ga marks it as the thing being said to be there.
One verb for two English sentences: 'there is a friend' and 'I have a friend' are both chingu-ga isseoyo. Korean does not separate having from existing; what exists takes -i or -ga.

sentences.trap: This one sentence is both 'I have a friend' and 'there is a friend', and Korean does not feel the difference. An English speaker will want two different sentences and will look for a verb meaning 'have'; there is not one here.
sentences.sound: CHIN-goo-ga i-SSUH-yo. The ss in isseoyo is tense — the tongue presses harder and the sound comes out tight, quite unlike the soft s of saram. That tension is a real contrast in Korean and it separates words.

variations.cue: I do not have a friend.
variations.changed: the opposite, and it is a different word rather than a negated one
a thing rather than a person — the same verb does both
two nouns stacked in front of the marker, as in M1

mistake.why: The object marker has been used for something that is not an object. Nothing is being acted on here — the friend simply exists — so the marker has to be -ga.

sentences.usage: Saying what you have, or what is there.
sentences.mnemonic: Korean does not have things; things simply are.

sentences.cue: There's no tea. There is coffee.

words.note: 'Tea', from M1. With -ga it is the thing that is there or missing; with -reul it is the thing drunk or not drunk.

words.cue: there is not · do not have
words.note: 'There is not', 'I do not have'. Its own word, NOT isseoyo with a negative attached — you cannot build it. Korean keeps a separate word for absence, which is why it is so short and common.
'Coffee', from M1 — here the thing that is there, so it takes -ga.
'There is', from the last sentence — the positive, set beside the absence verb so you hear that they are two words.

sentences.trap: Do not build this out of isseoyo. There is no negative particle in it and none can be added — eopseoyo is a separate word, and an isseoyo is not something a Korean speaker would say or recognise.
sentences.sound: CHA-ga UP-suh-yo. KUH-pee-ga i-SSUH-yo. The p sound inside eopseoyo is not released: the lips close and the next sound follows. Then a full stop, and the second sentence offers what there is instead.

variations.changed: a consonant-final noun, so the marker is -i
the positive alone, for comparison — two different words for two opposite facts
a different thing missing, and -i after the consonant

mistake.why: an has been put in front of isseoyo to build a negative. Korean does not negate this verb; it has a second verb for absence, and that verb is eopseoyo.

sentences.usage: Telling somebody you are out of something — and what there is instead.

words.note: 'I', in the polite style. It appears in these sentences only where the wanting needs an owner; where the situation already says who, Korean leaves it out.
'Tea', from M1. With -ga it is the thing that is there or missing; with -reul it is the thing drunk or not drunk.
'Not', and it goes in front of the verb — the one thing in a Korean sentence that does. Everything else attaches behind; an stands just before the verb it cancels: an meogeoyo.
'Drink'. Stem masi-; the plain -yo form and the -go shape before sipeoyo. The stem's i and the ending run together into masyeoyo — a normal contraction, written as it is said.

sentences.trap: an is the one piece in this course that goes in FRONT of what it belongs to. Every marker you have met attaches behind its word; this stands separately, immediately before the verb, and nothing may come between them.
sentences.sound: juh-nun CHA-rul an ma-SHUH-yo. an is a single light beat and it leans onto the verb after it, so an masyeoyo comes out almost as one word. masyeoyo has the sh sound because the stem's i colours the s in front of the following vowel.

variations.changed: a different drink refused
a different verb, and the subject dropped
the positive — an simply comes out, and nothing else changes

mistake.why: The negation has been put after the verb, where English would put 'not' after 'do'. an has exactly one seat and it is directly in front of the verb.

sentences.usage: Saying what you do not do, as a habit — jeo-neun is here because you are setting yourself apart from people who do.
sentences.mnemonic: an sits in front of the verb and nowhere else.

words.note: 'Cooked rice', and by extension a meal: bap meokgo sipeoyo is closer to 'I want to eat' than 'I want rice'. Korean counts the day in meals of bap as English does in breakfast and dinner.
'Not', and it goes in front of the verb — the one thing in a Korean sentence that does. Everything else attaches behind; an stands just before the verb it cancels: an meogeoyo.
'Eat'. Two shapes of one verb: meogeoyo is the plain -yo form used from the next module on; meokgo is the shape before sipeoyo. The stem is meok-, and everything happens to that.

sentences.trap: There is no subject here and none is missing, and no marker on bap either. English would need 'I'; supplying jeo-neun would turn the sentence into a contrast — as if somebody else were eating and you were not.
sentences.sound: bap an MUH-guh-yo. The held p of bap, then an leaning onto the verb. The k of the stem softens to a g between vowels, so meogeoyo runs smoothly; the word is still built on meok-, which is the shape you saw in meokgo.

variations.changed: the positive, with an taken out
the subject put back in, which now sounds like a contrast with somebody else
the negation now belongs to the wanting, and an moves in front of the whole thing

mistake.why: an has been put at the head of the sentence, where English puts 'not' in 'not eating'. It belongs immediately before the VERB, and the object stays in front of it.

sentences.usage: Turning down a meal, or saying you are skipping one.
sentences.mnemonic: Everything else in the sentence stays; an slips in front of the verb.

words.note: 'Coffee', from M1, wearing two new markers here: -do for 'coffee too' and -ga for coffee as the thing that exists.
One verb for two English sentences: 'there is a friend' and 'I have a friend' are both chingu-ga isseoyo. Korean does not separate having from existing; what exists takes -i or -ga.

sentences.trap: Asked in a cafe this means 'do you have coffee', and asked at home it means 'is there any coffee'. Korean does not choose between them, and neither should you: the situation decides what it means, not the words.
sentences.sound: KUH-pee-ga i-SSUH-yo, with the last syllable lifting. It is the same sentence as the statement with the same tense ss in the middle — the rise is doing all the questioning.

variations.changed: a different thing asked about
the negative question — and remember that ne answers 'right, there is none'
said flat, it is the answer rather than the question

mistake.why: The object marker again, on something that is not an object. Existence takes -i or -ga, question or not.

sentences.mnemonic: Ask for existence with -ga, never with -reul.

comprehensionPool.cue: I do not have a friend.
